chapters.title: 1. Key Functions of Water in Biochemistry and Physiology
chapters.content:
1. Key Functions of Water in Biochemistry and Physiology

Universal Solvent:

Dissolves ions, enzymes, and nutrients (e.g., glucose, amino acids) to enable metabolic reactions.

Facilitates hydrolysis reactions (e.g., breakdown of ATP, proteins, and carbohydrates).

Transport Medium:

Blood plasma (~90% water) transports oxygen, hormones, nutrients (e.g., glucose, fatty acids), and waste products (e.g., urea, CO₂).

Lymphatic fluid and interstitial fluid rely on water for nutrient exchange between cells.

Thermoregulation:

Sweat evaporates to cool the body during heat or exercise, maintaining enzyme function and cellular integrity.

Structural Role:

Maintains cell turgor pressure (critical for plant and animal cells).

Lubricates joints (synovial fluid), eyes (tears), and digestive tract (mucus).

Electrolyte Balance:

Regulates osmotic pressure and pH balance (e.g., bicarbonate buffering in blood).

Enables nerve impulse transmission and muscle contraction via sodium-potassium pumps.

Waste Removal:

Kidneys use water to filter and excrete metabolic waste (urea, creatinine) via urine.

chapters.title: 6. Regulation of Water Balance
chapters.content:
6. Regulation of Water Balance

Hormonal Control:

Antidiuretic hormone (ADH): Signals kidneys to retain water.

Aldosterone: Promotes sodium (and thus water) reabsorption.

Thirst mechanism: Hypothalamus triggers thirst when blood osmolarity rises.

Conclusion

Water is the ultimate "silent nutrient" – it doesn’t provide energy, but life ceases within days without it. Its roles in biochemistry (solvent, reactant, transporter) and physiology (temperature, structure, waste removal) make it the cornerstone of metabolic health. Understanding water’s interplay with electrolytes, hormones, and organ systems is critical in nutrition science and clinical care.

CARBOHYRATE

Carbohydrates are one of the three macronutrients in the human diet, along with protein and fat. These molecules contain carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms. Carbohydrates play an important role in the human body. They act as an energy source, help control blood glucose and insulin metabolism, participate in cholesterol and triglyceride metabolism, and help with fermentation. The digestive tract begins to break down carbohydrates into glucose, which is used for energy upon consumption. Any extra glucose in the bloodstream is stored in the liver and muscle tissue until further energy is needed. Carbohydrates is an umbrella term that encompasses sugar, fruits, vegetables, fibers, and legumes. While there are numerous divisions of carbohydrates, the human diet benefits mostly from a certain subset. 

Carbohydrates can be classified into several types based on their chemical structure and complexity. Here's a breakdown of the main types of carbohydrates:

chapters.title: 1. Monosaccharides (Simple Sugars)
chapters.content:
1. Monosaccharides (Simple Sugars)

Monosaccharides are the simplest form of carbohydrates, consisting of a single sugar molecule. They are the basic building blocks for more complex carbohydrates.

Glucose: The most common monosaccharide and a primary source of energy for cells. It’s found in foods like fruits and vegetables and is often referred to as "blood sugar."

Fructose: Found mainly in fruits, honey, and root vegetables. It is the sweetest of the monosaccharides.

Galactose: Less sweet than glucose and fructose, it is primarily found in dairy products as part of the disaccharide lactose.

chapters.title: 2. Disaccharides (Two Sugar Units)
chapters.content:
2. Disaccharides (Two Sugar Units)

Disaccharides are formed when two monosaccharides join together through a glycosidic bond. These sugars must be broken down into monosaccharides before they can be absorbed and used by the body.

Sucrose: Common table sugar, made of glucose and fructose. It’s found in sugar cane, beets, and many fruits.

Lactose: The sugar found in milk, composed of glucose and galactose. It’s broken down in the body by the enzyme lactase.

Maltose: Formed from two glucose molecules. It’s produced during the breakdown of starch and is found in malted grains and products like beer.

chapters.title: 4. Polysaccharides (Complex Carbohydrates)
chapters.content:
4. Polysaccharides (Complex Carbohydrates)

Polysaccharides are long chains of monosaccharide units, often hundreds or thousands of sugar molecules long. They serve as storage forms of energy or provide structural support in plants and animals.

Starch: The primary storage form of carbohydrates in plants, found in foods like potatoes, rice, corn, and wheat. It is made up of long chains of glucose molecules.

Glycogen: The storage form of glucose in animals, primarily stored in the liver and muscles. It’s similar to starch but more highly branched.

Cellulose: A structural polysaccharide that makes up the cell walls of plants. It is composed of glucose molecules but is indigestible by humans due to its unique bonding structure. It’s important for digestive health as dietary fiber.

chapters.title: 5. Fiber
chapters.content:
5. Fiber

Fiber is a type of carbohydrate that the human digestive system cannot fully break down. It plays a key role in digestive health, helping to regulate bowel movements and lower cholesterol levels. Fiber is primarily found in plant foods like fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and legumes. There are two types of dietary fiber:

Soluble Fiber: Dissolves in water to form a gel-like substance. It helps lower cholesterol and regulate blood sugar. Found in foods like oats, beans, apples, and carrots.

Insoluble Fiber: Does not dissolve in water and helps add bulk to stool, aiding in digestion and preventing constipation. Found in foods like whole wheat, nuts, and vegetables.

Summary

Simple Carbohydrates: Monosaccharides (e.g., glucose, fructose, galactose) and disaccharides (e.g., sucrose, lactose, maltose).

Complex Carbohydrates: Oligosaccharides and polysaccharides (e.g., starch, glycogen, cellulose).

Dietary Fiber: Soluble and insoluble fiber, which contribute to digestive health.

Each type of carbohydrate serves a different function in the body, from providing quick energy (simple sugars) to offering long-lasting energy storage and fiber for digestive health (complex carbohydrates).

FUNCTIONS OF CARBOHYDRATES IN THE HUMAN BODY

chapters.title: 1. Digestion and Absorption
chapters.content:
1. Digestion and Absorption

Digestion: Begins in the mouth with salivary amylase breaking down starch into smaller polysaccharides. Pancreatic amylase in the small intestine further breaks these into disaccharides, which are then hydrolyzed by brush-border enzymes (e.g., lactase, sucrase) into monosaccharides.

Absorption: Monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, galactose) are absorbed in the small intestine via specific transporters:

SGLT1: Sodium-glucose cotransporter for glucose and galactose.

GLUT5: Facilitates fructose absorption.

chapters.title: 2. Metabolic Pathways
chapters.content:
2. Metabolic Pathways

Carbohydrates are central to energy metabolism through the following pathways:

Glycolysis: Glucose is broken down into pyruvate, producing ATP and NADH.

Citric Acid Cycle (TCA Cycle): Pyruvate enters the mitochondria, is converted to acetyl-CoA, and fuels the TCA cycle for ATP production.

Gluconeogenesis: Synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors (e.g., amino acids, glycerol) during fasting or low-carb intake.

Glycogenesis: Excess glucose is stored as glycogen in the liver and muscles.

Glycogenolysis: Breakdown of glycogen to release glucose when energy is needed.

chapters.title: 12. Research and Trends
chapters.content:
12. Research and Trends

Low-Carb Diets: Keto and paleo diets are popular but require careful planning to avoid nutrient deficiencies.

Personalized Nutrition: Genetic and microbiome research is exploring individualized carbohydrate needs.

In summary, carbohydrates are indispensable in nutritional biochemistry, serving as a primary energy source, regulating blood glucose, and contributing to structural and signaling roles in the body. A balanced intake of high-quality carbohydrates is essential for optimal health

 Functions of carbohydrate in Nutrition

Energy Production:

Glucose is the preferred fuel for the brain, red blood cells, and muscles.

Stored as glycogen in the liver and muscles for short-term energy needs.

Gut Health:

Fiber promotes healthy gut microbiota, prevents constipation, and may reduce colon cancer risk.

Prebiotics (e.g., FOS) stimulate growth of beneficial bacteria (e.g., Bifidobacteria).

Blood Sugar Regulation:

Complex carbs (whole grains, legumes) release glucose slowly, preventing spikes.

Simple sugars (soda, candy) cause rapid blood sugar fluctuations.

Cholesterol Management:

Soluble fiber binds bile acids, lowering LDL ("bad" cholesterol).

Weight Management:

High-fiber foods increase satiety, reducing overeating.

Dietary Sources

Healthy Carbs:

Whole grains (oats, quinoa, brown rice).

Fruits (berries, apples, oranges).

Vegetables (leafy greens, broccoli, carrots).

Legumes (beans, lentils, chickpeas).

Less Healthy Carbs:

Refined sugars (soda, candy, pastries).

Refined grains (white bread, white rice).

chapters.title: 5. Health Considerations
chapters.content:
5. Health Considerations

Added Sugars vs. Natural Sugars:

Added sugars (e.g., sucrose in desserts) are linked to obesity, diabetes, and heart disease.

Natural sugars (e.g., fructose in fruit) come with fiber, vitamins, and antioxidants.

Glycemic Index (GI):

Measures how quickly a carb raises blood sugar. Low-GI foods (e.g., lentils) are healthier.

Carbohydrate Intolerance:

Lactose intolerance: Inability to digest lactose due to lactase deficiency.

FODMAP Sensitivity: Some people react poorly to fermentable carbs (e.g., onions, garlic).

chapters.title: 7. Special Diets
chapters.content:
7. Special Diets

Low-Carb Diets (e.g., keto, Atkins): Restrict carbs to induce ketosis (fat burning).

High-Carb Diets: Common in athletes for glycogen replenishment.

Key Takeaway

Carbohydrates are not inherently "bad"—their quality and source matter. Prioritize whole, unprocessed carbs (fruits, vegetables, whole grains) over refined sugars and starches to support long-term health.

What Is the Glycemic Index?

The GI is a rating system that ranks carbohydrates on a scale of 1 to 100 based on how much they raise blood sugar. Processed foods such as candy, breads, cake, and cookies have a high GI, while whole foods such as unrefined grains, non-starchy vegetables, and fruits tend to have a lower GI.

Carbohydrates with a low GI value are digested, absorbed, and metabolized more slowly than their high-GI counterparts. They typically cause a lower and slower rise in blood glucose and, subsequently, insulin levels as well. Foods that are primarily fat or protein are not included in the index because they have a minimal impact on blood sugar levels.

Glycemic Index Chart for Common Foods

The GI values can be broken down into three ranges. Food with a low GI is a food that won't raise your blood sugar as much as a food with a medium or high GI.1

Low GI: 55 or less

Medium GI: 56 to 69

High GI: 70 to 100

How Glycemic Index Is Measured

Glycem	ic index values were developed by a rigorous testing process using 10 or more people for each food.

Researchers measured blood sugar levels of healthy volunteers before and two-hours after eating 50 grams of the same digestible carbohydrate (the test food). The points were then plotted on a graph and researchers determined the area under the curve (AUC) of their glucose response.

At a separate date, the same 10 people consumed 50 grams of pure glucose (the reference food), and researchers again measured each person's glucose response AUC two hours after consumption.

The GI value of the test food is then calculated by dividing the glucose AUC for the test food by that of the reference food for each person. The final GI value is an average of those 10 numbers.

Ultimately, the GI value is the average person's blood sugar response to a specific carbohydrate. Individual responses may vary based on other factors including other foods eaten in combination with the carbohydrate.

Benefits of Referring to the Glycemic Index

Since it's the carbohydrates in food that raise blood sugar, understanding GI can help you figure out which foods are best for glucose management.5

Among the benefits of following the GI list when planning your meals:

It helps you be more mindful of your carb choices without fully restricting or severely limiting your intake.

If you aim for a low-GI diet, you'll naturally be focusing on whole grains, fruits, vegetables, and legumes, as opposed to the higher-GI end of the spectrum, which includes more processed foods.

Depending on your health goals, following a GI-based diet might mean you'll be able to rely less on standard dieting measures, such as calorie counting or regimented portion control.

Simply being more mindful of your carb choices rather than severely limiting them can also be more sustainable in the long run, as compared to more restrictive diets.

PROTEIN

Protein is a large, complex macromolecule made up of one or more long chains of amino acids linked together by peptide bonds. In nutrition biochemistry, proteins are essential not only as a key dietary macronutrient but also for nearly every cellular function. 

Their specific sequence of amino acids—encoded by genes—determines how they fold into unique three-dimensional structures, which in turn dictate their roles in the body. These roles include acting as enzymes to catalyze biochemical reactions, serving as structural components (such as collagen in connective tissue), functioning as hormones and signaling molecules (like insulin), and helping to transport substances (such as hemoglobin carrying oxygen) throughout the body. In essence, proteins are the building blocks and workhorses of cells, critical for growth, repair, and overall health.

Protein is a vital part of the human diet. The protein content for example Muscles contain about 30 percent protein, the liver 20 to 30 percent, and red blood cells 30 percent. Higher percentages of protein are found in hair, bones, and other organs and tissues with a low water content.

Classification of proteins

chapters.title: 1. Protein Structure
chapters.content:
1. Protein Structure

Proteins are made up of amino acids (AAs), the building blocks of life. Their structure determines their function and nutritional quality.

A. Amino Acids

Essential AAs (EAAs): Cannot be synthesized by the body; must be obtained from food (9 total: histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, valine).

Non-Essential AAs: Can be synthesized by the body.

Conditionally Essential AAs: Required in certain conditions (e.g., illness, stress).

B. Protein Structure Levels

Primary Structure: Linear sequence of amino acids.

Secondary Structure: Local folding into alpha-helices or beta-sheets (e.g., collagen).

Tertiary Structure: 3D shape of a single polypeptide chain.

Quaternary Structure: Multiple polypeptide chains interacting (e.g., hemoglobin).

C. Complete vs. Incomplete Proteins

Complete Proteins: Contain all 9 EAAs in sufficient amounts (e.g., animal proteins, soy, quinoa).

Incomplete Proteins: Lack one or more EAAs (e.g., most plant proteins).

Complementary Proteins: Combining incomplete proteins (e.g., rice + beans) to provide all EAAs.

chapters.title: 2. Protein Digestibility
chapters.content:
2. Protein Digestibility

Digestibility refers to how well the body can break down and absorb protein from food.

A. Factors Affecting Digestibility

Protein Source:

Animal proteins (e.g., eggs, whey) are generally more digestible than plant proteins (e.g., legumes, grains).

Processing:

Cooking improves digestibility by denaturing proteins (e.g., raw eggs vs. cooked eggs).

Fermentation (e.g., tempeh) and sprouting (e.g., sprouted grains) enhance plant protein digestibility.

Anti-Nutritional Factors:

Compounds like phytates (in grains) and trypsin inhibitors (in legumes) reduce digestibility.

Soaking, fermenting, or cooking reduces these factors.

B. Measures of Digestibility

Protein Digestibility-Corrected Amino Acid Score (PDCAAS):

Gold standard for protein quality (scale: 0–1).

Accounts for both amino acid profile and digestibility.

Example: Whey protein = 1.0, soy protein = 0.91, lentils = 0.52.

Digestible Indispensable Amino Acid Score (DIAAS):

Newer method, more accurate for assessing protein quality.

chapters.title: 3. Protein Bioavailability
chapters.content:
3. Protein Bioavailability

Bioavailability refers to how well the body can use the absorbed protein for metabolic processes.

A. Factors Affecting Bioavailability

Amino Acid Composition:

Proteins with a balanced EAA profile (e.g., leucine-rich whey) are more bioavailable.

Digestibility:

Higher digestibility = higher bioavailability.

Food Matrix:

Presence of fiber, fat, or other nutrients can slow absorption.

Individual Factors:

Age, gut health, and metabolic state influence bioavailability.

B. Enhancing Bioavailability

Pairing Proteins: Combining complementary proteins (e.g., rice + beans) improves EAA availability.

Timing: Consuming protein post-workout enhances muscle protein synthesis.

Processing: Hydrolyzed proteins (pre-digested) are more bioavailable.

Types of Proteins

chapters.title: 1. By Molecular Function
chapters.content:
1. By Molecular Function

Proteins in our bodies are not just nutrients—they perform a vast range of biological roles. Functionally, they can be grouped as follows:

Enzymatic Proteins:
– Act as catalysts to speed up chemical reactions (e.g., digestive enzymes like amylase or proteases).

Hormonal Proteins:
– Serve as messengers that coordinate bodily functions (e.g., insulin regulates blood sugar).

Structural Proteins:
– Provide support and shape to cells and tissues (e.g., collagen in skin and connective tissue; keratin in hair and nails).

Transport Proteins:
– Carry molecules within the body (e.g., hemoglobin transports oxygen; albumin carries various substances in the blood).

Defensive Proteins:
– Protect the body against pathogens (e.g., antibodies of the immune system).

Contractile Proteins: in movement and muscle contraction (e.g., actin and myosin in muscle fibers).

Storage Proteins: Serve as reserves of amino acids or minerals (e.g., casein in milk or ferritin which stores iron).

Receptor Proteins:Located on cell surfaces, they bind signaling molecules to trigger cellular responses (e.g., insulin receptors).

This eight-category system highlights how proteins act as the “workhorses” of the cell, with each group playing an essential role in maintaining health and function.

chapters.title: 3. By Structural Characteristics
chapters.content:
3. By Structural Characteristics

On the molecular level, proteins can also be classified by their three-dimensional shape and solubility:

Globular Proteins:
• Generally compact and spherical in shape.
• They are often water-soluble and include most enzymes and transport proteins.

Fibrous Proteins:
• Long and filamentous, typically forming structural components in the body (e.g., collagen, elastin, keratin).
• They are usually insoluble in water and help provide strength and support.

Membrane Proteins:
• Embedded in or associated with cell membranes.
• They serve critical roles in transport, signaling, and cell–cell interactions.

In Summary

Dietary Perspective: You have animal, plant, and alternative protein sources.

Functional Perspective: Proteins are grouped by roles such as enzymes, hormones, structural, transport, defensive, contractile, storage, and receptor proteins.

Structural Perspective: Proteins are often described as globular, fibrous, or membrane proteins based on their three-dimensional structure and solubility.

Each of these classifications provides a different lens for understanding protein’s vital role in both nutrition and cellular biology. Choosing the right type of protein—whether for a balanced diet or for specific functional benefits—depends on these properties as well as your personal health goals.

chapters.title: 6. Practical Tips for Optimal Protein Nutrition
chapters.content:
6. Practical Tips for Optimal Protein Nutrition

Diversify Sources: Include both animal (e.g., eggs, fish, dairy) and plant proteins (e.g., legumes, nuts, seeds).

Prioritize Quality: Choose high-PDCAAS/DIAAS proteins (e.g., whey, soy, eggs).

Optimize Digestibility: Cook, ferment, or sprout plant proteins to reduce anti-nutritional factors.

Spread Intake: Distribute protein across meals (e.g., 20–30 g per meal) for optimal muscle synthesis.

Supplement Wisely: Use protein powders (e.g., whey, pea) if dietary intake is insufficient.

 Why Protein Needs Increase in Stress

Hyper catabolism: Stress (e.g., trauma, surgery, burns, sepsis) triggers muscle breakdown to supply amino acids for:

Wound healing,

Immune function (antibodies, cytokines),

Acute-phase protein synthesis (e.g., C-reactive protein).

Nitrogen Loss: Negative nitrogen balance occurs as protein breakdown exceeds synthesis.

Hypermetabolism: Metabolic rate increases by 20–100% (e.g., severe burns increase demands by 150%).

chapters.title: 3. Key Considerations
chapters.content:
3. Key Considerations

A. Amino Acid Priorities

Essential Amino Acids (EAAs): Critical for muscle preservation and repair.

Branched-Chain Amino Acids (BCAAs):

Leucine: Stimulates muscle protein synthesis.

Isoleucine/Valine: Reduce muscle breakdown.

Conditionally Essential AAs:

Glutamine: Gut integrity, immune support (often depleted in critical illness).

Arginine: Enhances wound healing and immune response.

B. Protein Quality

High Biological Value (HBV) Proteins:

Whey, casein, eggs, or soy (rapidly absorbed, rich in EAAs).

Hydrolyzed Proteins/Peptides: Better absorbed in critically ill patients with gut dysfunction.

C. Timing and Delivery

Early Enteral Nutrition: Start within 24–48 hours of trauma/critical illness to preserve gut function.

Continuous vs. Bolus Feeding: Continuous feeding optimizes absorption in hypermetabolic states.

Parenteral Nutrition: Reserved for patients unable to tolerate enteral feeding.

chapters.title: 7. Risks of Overfeeding
chapters.content:
7. Risks of Overfeeding

Uremia: Excess protein in renal impairment.

Hyperammonemia: In hepatic dysfunction.

Metabolic Stress: Overfeeding carbs/fats can worsen hyperglycemia or hypertriglyceridemia.

Practical Recommendations

Prioritize HBV Proteins: Whey, eggs, or soy isolates in enteral formulas.

Supplement Glutamine/BCAAs: In burns, trauma, or sepsis (under clinical guidance).

Adjust for Organ Dysfunction: Use specialized formulas (e.g., BCAA-enriched for liver failure).

Combine with Calories: Ensure adequate non-protein calories (25–30 kcal/kg/day) to spare protein for synthesis.

summary

In stress, trauma, or critical illness, protein needs rise sharply to counteract catabolism and support recovery. Tailor intake to the patient’s condition, prioritize high-quality proteins, and monitor closely to optimize outcomes. Always balance protein delivery with metabolic tolerance and organ function.

DIGESTION OF PROTEINS: PROCESS AND ENZYMES INVOLVED

Protein digestion is a complex process that involves mechanical breakdown, enzymatic hydrolysis, and absorption of amino acids. It begins in the mouth, continues in the stomach, and is completed in the small intestine with the help of digestive enzymes.

chapters.title: 2. Step-by-Step Digestion of Proteins
chapters.content:
2. Step-by-Step Digestion of Proteins

(A) In the Mouth (Mechanical Digestion)

No chemical digestion of proteins occurs in the mouth.

Chewing (mastication) breaks proteins into smaller fragments, increasing the surface area for enzyme action.

(B) In the Stomach (Chemical Digestion Begins)

The stomach secretes gastric juice, which contains:

Hydrochloric acid (HCl):

Lowers the stomach pH (1.5–3.5), denaturing proteins (unfolding their structure).

Activates pepsinogen → pepsin (an enzyme that digests proteins).

Pepsin:

Breaks down large protein molecules into smaller peptides.

Works best in the acidic environment of the stomach.

(C) In the Small Intestine (Major Protein Digestion)

The pancreas secretes enzymes into the small intestine to continue digestion.

Enzymes involved:

Trypsin & Chymotrypsin (from pancreas): Break proteins into smaller peptides.

Carboxypeptidase: Removes individual amino acids from the peptide chains.

Peptidases (from intestinal lining): Break short peptides into free amino acids for absorption.

(D) Absorption of Amino Acids

Free amino acids are absorbed through the intestinal lining into the bloodstream.

Transported to the liver via the hepatic portal vein, where they are processed for:

Protein synthesis

Energy production

Conversion into other compounds (e.g., neurotransmitters, hormones)

chapters.title: 4. End Products of Protein Digestion
chapters.content:
4. End Products of Protein Digestion

Conclusion

Protein digestion is a well-regulated process involving the stomach, pancreas, and small intestine. It ensures that proteins from food are broken down into amino acids, which are absorbed and used for body functions such as muscle repair, enzyme production, and immune support.

UTILIZATION OF PROTEINS IN THE BODY

After digestion, proteins are broken down into amino acids, which are then absorbed, transported, and utilized for various physiological functions. These amino acids serve as the building blocks for body tissues, enzymes, hormones, and other essential compounds.

chapters.title: 1. Stages of Protein Utilization
chapters.content:
1. Stages of Protein Utilization

The process of protein utilization includes:

Absorption & Transport – Amino acids enter the bloodstream and travel to tissues.

Protein Synthesis – Amino acids are used to build new proteins.

Energy Production (If Needed) – Proteins can be converted into glucose or energy.

Conversion into Other Molecules – Some amino acids are transformed into neurotransmitters, hormones, or nitrogen-containing compounds.

Excretion of Excess Nitrogen – Unused nitrogen is excreted as urea in urine.

chapters.title: 2. Protein Utilization Pathways
chapters.content:
2. Protein Utilization Pathways

(A) Absorption and Transport

After digestion, amino acids are absorbed into the bloodstream through the small intestine.

Transported via the hepatic portal vein to the liver for processing.

(B) Protein Synthesis (Anabolism)

The primary function of amino acids is protein synthesis, which occurs in cells.

Types of proteins synthesized:

Structural Proteins: Muscle fibers, collagen, keratin (skin, hair, nails).

Functional Proteins: Enzymes, hormones (insulin, growth hormone), antibodies.

Transport Proteins: Hemoglobin (oxygen transport), albumin (nutrient transport).

(C) Energy Production from Proteins (Catabolism)

If the body lacks carbohydrates and fats, amino acids can be converted into energy through gluconeogenesis.

Steps:

Deamination: Removal of the amino group (-NH₂) from the amino acid.

Conversion to Glucose or Fat: The remaining carbon skeleton is used for glucose (gluconeogenesis) or fat storage.

ATP Production: Some amino acids enter the Krebs cycle to generate ATP.

(D) Conversion into Other Important Compounds

Hormones: Amino acids are precursors to insulin, glucagon, thyroid hormones.

Neurotransmitters: Tryptophan → Serotonin, Tyrosine → Dopamine & Adrenaline.

Nitrogen-containing Compounds: Used to make DNA, RNA, creatine, and heme (in hemoglobin).

(E) Excretion of Excess Nitrogen

Amino groups removed during deamination form ammonia (NH₃).

Ammonia is toxic and is converted into urea in the liver.

Urea is transported to the kidneys and excreted in urine.

chapters.title: 4. Factors Affecting Protein Utilization
chapters.content:
4. Factors Affecting Protein Utilization

Protein Quality: Animal proteins (meat, eggs, dairy) have all essential amino acids, while plant proteins (legumes, grains) may lack some.

Metabolic Needs: Growing children, athletes, and pregnant women need more protein.

Carbohydrate & Fat Intake: If carbs and fats are insufficient, the body breaks down protein for energy.

Health Conditions: Liver or kidney diseases affect protein metabolism and nitrogen excretion.

Conclusion

Protein utilization is essential for growth, repair, metabolism, and immune function. While protein synthesis is the primary role, excess protein can be used for energy or converted into other important molecules. Proper protein intake is crucial for maintaining muscle mass, hormonal balance, and overall health.

LIPIDS

Lipids are a diverse group of naturally occurring organic compounds that are primarily characterized by their hydrophobic (water‐repelling) or amphipathic (having both hydrophobic and hydrophilic regions) properties. In practical terms, this means that lipids are generally insoluble in water but soluble in non‐polar solvents like chloroform or ether.

Key points about lipids include:

• Diversity of Types:
 Lipids include fats (triglycerides), oils, waxes, phospholipids, sterols (such as cholesterol), and fat‐soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K).
 Each of these classes plays different roles, from energy storage (triglycerides) to forming the bilayer structure of cell membranes (phospholipids and cholesterol).

• Biological Functions:
 – Energy Storage: Lipids serve as a dense energy reserve, providing more than twice the energy per gram compared to carbohydrates.
 – Structural Components: Phospholipids and cholesterol are essential for the formation and maintenance of cell membranes, helping to regulate permeability and cell signaling.
 – Signaling Molecules: Certain lipids act as hormones (for example, steroid hormones) or signaling mediators that regulate a variety of physiological processes.
 – Insulation and Protection: Lipids also help insulate the body and protect organs.

• Chemical Characteristics:
 Lipids are not polymers in the classical sense—they are not formed by a repeated linking of identical monomers via dehydration synthesis (as proteins or nucleic acids are). Instead, they are a heterogeneous group of compounds that share a general insolubility in water due to their long hydrocarbon chains.

Lipids are a diverse group of hydrophobic or amphipathic molecules that play many essential roles in biology, from energy storage to cell structure and signaling. They are not defined by a single chemical structure but rather by their general insolubility in water. In general, lipids can be classified into several main groups:

Simple Lipids:

 • Triglycerides (Fats and Oils): These are esters formed from one molecule of glycerol and three fatty acids. They serve primarily as energy storage molecules and can be found as solid fats (saturated fats, common in animal fats) or as oils (unsaturated fats, common in plant oils).

 • Waxes: Composed of long-chain fatty acids esterified to long-chain alcohols, waxes serve as protective coatings on leaves, fruits, and animal surfaces (like earwax).

Compound Lipids:

 • Phospholipids: These contain glycerol, two fatty acids, a phosphate group, and a polar head group. They are the main building blocks of cell membranes, forming a lipid bilayer that provides structure and regulates the movement of substances into and out of cells.

 • Glycolipids: Similar to phospholipids but with one or more sugar molecules attached, glycolipids are also important components of cell membranes, particularly in nerve tissue and for cell recognition.

 • Sphingolipids: Built on a sphingosine backbone rather than glycerol, these lipids (which include sphingomyelin and cerebrosides) are important for forming the myelin sheath around nerve cells and play roles in signal transduction.

Derived (Complex) Lipids:

 • Sterols: The most well-known example is cholesterol, which is vital for maintaining cell membrane integrity, serves as a precursor for steroid hormones (such as estrogen and testosterone), bile acids, and vitamin D.

 • Fat-Soluble Vitamins: While not lipids in the strict structural sense, vitamins A, D, E, and K are lipid-soluble and are transported within the body along with other fats.

Each class of lipid has unique properties and functions that contribute to overall health. For instance, while triglycerides provide energy, an imbalance (especially high levels of saturated or trans fats) can raise blood cholesterol levels and increase the risk of cardiovascular disease. In contrast, unsaturated fats—found in many plant oils and fatty fish—tend to support heart health.

chapters.title: 3. Fatty Acids: The Building Blocks
chapters.content:
3. Fatty Acids: The Building Blocks

Fatty acids (FAs) are key components of most lipids. They are classified by:

A. Saturation

Saturated FAs: No double bonds (e.g., palmitic acid in butter). Solid at room temperature.

Unsaturated FAs:

Monounsaturated (MUFA): 1 double bond (e.g., oleic acid in olive oil).

Polyunsaturated (PUFA): ≥2 double bonds (e.g., omega-3 in fish, omega-6 in seeds).

B. Essential Fatty Acids

Omega-3 (α-linolenic acid): Found in fish, flaxseed, walnuts. Supports brain health, reduces inflammation.

Omega-6 (linoleic acid): Found in vegetable oils. Important for skin integrity, but excess may promote inflammation.

chapters.title: 4. Functions of Lipids in the Body
chapters.content:
4. Functions of Lipids in the Body

Energy Storage: Triglycerides store energy in adipose tissue (1 kg fat ≈ 7,700 kcal).

Cell Membranes: Phospholipids and cholesterol form the lipid bilayer, regulating permeability and fluidity.

Hormone Synthesis: Cholesterol is a precursor for steroid hormones (e.g., cortisol, estrogen, testosterone).

Insulation & Protection: Adipose tissue cushions organs and insulates the body.

Absorption of Fat-Soluble Vitamins: Vitamins A, D, E, and K require dietary fat for absorption.

Signaling: Eicosanoids regulate inflammation, blood clotting, and blood pressure.

chapters.title: 7.Digestion & Absorption
chapters.content:
7.Digestion & Absorption

A. Mouth

Mechanical breakdown: Chewing breaks fat into smaller droplets.

Lingual lipase: An enzyme secreted by salivary glands begins breaking down triglycerides (TGs) into diglycerides and free fatty acids (FFAs). However, this enzyme is more active in the acidic stomach environment.

B. Stomach

Gastric lipase: Continues hydrolyzing TGs into diglycerides and FFAs.

Churning: Further emulsifies fats into smaller droplets.

C. Small Intestine (Primary site of fat digestion)

Emulsification:

Bile salts (from the liver, stored in the gallbladder) coat fat droplets, breaking them into tiny micelles (1–2 µm). This increases the surface area for enzymes to act.

Enzymatic digestion:

Pancreatic lipase: The main enzyme that hydrolyzes TGs into 2-monoglycerides and FFAs.

Colipase: A coenzyme that anchors pancreatic lipase to the micelle surface.

Cholesterol esterase: Breaks cholesterol esters into free cholesterol and FFAs.

Phospholipase A2: Breaks phospholipids into lysophospholipids and FFAs.

chapters.title: 2. Absorption of Fats
chapters.content:
2. Absorption of Fats

Micelle formation:

Bile salts, FFAs, monoglycerides, cholesterol, and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) form mixed micelles. These transport hydrophobic lipids to the intestinal lining (enterocytes).

Uptake by enterocytes:

Lipids diffuse passively across the cell membrane of the small intestine.

Reassembly in enterocytes:

FFAs and monoglycerides are re-esterified into new triglycerides.

Cholesterol and phospholipids are repackaged.

Chylomicron formation:

Triglycerides, cholesterol, and fat-soluble vitamins combine with apolipoprotein B-48 to form chylomicrons (large lipoprotein particles).

chapters.title: 8. Health Implications
chapters.content:
8. Health Implications

Cardiovascular Disease: Excessive consumption of saturated fats and trans fats can raise low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, often referred to as "bad" cholesterol, which is linked to atherosclerosis and an increased risk of heart disease and stroke. Diets that are high in these fats have been associated with coronary heart disease. 

Obesity: Excess calorie intake from fats contributes to weight gain. High intakes of dietary fats contribute to an overall high-calorie diet. When energy intake consistently exceeds expenditure, weight gain and obesity can occur. Obesity is a well-known risk factor for type 2 diabetes, certain cancers, and other metabolic disorders.

Inflammation: Omega-3s reduce inflammation, while excess omega-6s may promote it. A disproportionate intake of omega-6 to omega-3 fatty acids can promote a pro-inflammatory state. While omega-6 polyunsaturated fats (found in many seed oils) are essential, an excessively high ratio relative to omega-3s may contribute to chronic inflammation, which is implicated in a range of conditions including arthritis and heart disease.

Essential Fatty Acid Deficiency: Rare but causes dry skin, impaired wound healing, and cognitive issues.

Dietary Recommendations and Balance

The key to reaping the benefits of lipids while minimizing their risks is balance and quality:

Choose Unsaturated Fats: Emphasize sources of monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats such as olive oil, avocado oil, fatty fish, nuts, and seeds.

Moderation in Saturated Fats: Limit high intakes of saturated fats from sources like red meat and certain full-fat dairy products, especially if other risk factors for heart disease exist.

Avoid Trans Fats: Reduce or eliminate intake of artificial trans fats found in many processed foods.

Overall Dietary Pattern: A diet that focuses on whole, minimally processed foods—such as those found in the Mediterranean diet—helps ensure a healthy balance of lipids along with essential vitamins, minerals, and fiber.

chapters.title: 9. Dietary Recommendations
chapters.content:
9. Dietary Recommendations

Total Fat: 20–35% of daily calories (varies by individual needs).

Saturated Fats: <10% of calories (WHO guideline).

Trans Fats: Avoid industrially produced trans fats.

Prioritize: Unsaturated fats (avocados, nuts, fish) over saturated/trans fats.

Lipids are indispensable for energy, cell structure, and hormone production, but their quality and quantity in the diet matter. Focus on unsaturated fats, limit saturated/trans fats, and ensure adequate intake of essential fatty acids (omega-3s) for optimal health.

Role of Lipids in Food: High Energy Source

Fat-rich foods naturally have a high caloric density. Foods that are high in fat contain more calories than foods high in protein or carbohydrates. As a result, high-fat foods are a convenient source of energy. For example, 1 gram of fat or oil provides 9 kilocalories of energy, compared with 4 kilocalories found in 1 gram of carbohydrate or protein. Depending on the level of physical activity and nutritional needs, fat requirements vary greatly from person to person. When energy needs are high, the body welcomes the high-caloric density of fats. For instance, infants and growing children require proper amounts of fat to support normal growth and development. If an infant or child is given a low-fat diet for an extended period, growth and development will not progress normally. Other individuals with high-energy needs are athletes, people who have physically demanding jobs, and those recuperating from illness.

When the body has used all of its calories from carbohydrates (this can occur after just twenty minutes of exercise), it initiates fat usage. A professional swimmer must consume large amounts of food energy to meet the demands of swimming long distances, so eating fat-rich foods makes sense. In contrast, if a person who leads a sedentary lifestyle eats the same high-density fat foods, they will intake more fat calories than their body requires within just a few bites. Use caution—consumption of calories over and beyond energy requirements is a contributing factor to obesity.

Role of Lipids in Food: Smell and Taste

Fat contains dissolved compounds that contribute to mouth-watering aromas and flavors and increase the palatability of food. Fat also adds texture to food. Baked foods are supple and moist. Frying foods locks in flavor and lessens cooking time. How long does it take you to recall the smell of your favorite food cooking? What would a meal be without that savory aroma to delight your senses and heighten your preparedness for eating a meal?

Fat plays another valuable role in nutrition. Fat contributes to satiety or the sensation of fullness. When fatty foods are swallowed the body responds by enabling the processes controlling digestion to retard the movement of food along the digestive tract, thus promoting an overall sense of fullness. Oftentimes before the feeling of fullness arrives, people overindulge in fat-rich foods, finding the delectable taste irresistible. Indeed, the very things that make fat-rich foods attractive also make them a hindrance to maintaining a healthful diet.

Triglycerides

Triglycerides: Overview, Function, and Health Implications

Triglycerides are a type of fat (lipid) found in the blood and are a crucial part of human metabolism. They serve as the body's main form of stored energy. When you consume more calories than needed, the body converts the excess into triglycerides and stores them in fat cells for future use.

Structure and Composition

Triglycerides consist of:

One glycerol molecule (a three-carbon alcohol)

Three fatty acid chains (which can be saturated or unsaturated)

Function of Triglycerides

Energy Storage – Triglycerides serve as the body's long-term energy reserve, stored in adipose (fat) tissue.

Insulation and Protection – Fat deposits help cushion organs and provide insulation against cold temperatures.

Metabolic Role – When energy is required, triglycerides are broken down into fatty acids and glycerol, which are used for energy production.

Triglycerides and Health Risks

While triglycerides are essential, excessively high levels can lead to various health problems, including:

Heart Disease – High triglyceride levels are associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular diseases.

Pancreatitis – Extremely high triglycerides (above 500 mg/dL) can lead to inflammation of the pancreas.

Metabolic Syndrome – A cluster of conditions (high blood pressure, obesity, high blood sugar, and high triglycerides) that increase the risk of diabetes and stroke.

Causes of High Triglycerides

Poor Diet – High sugar, refined carbs, and unhealthy fats contribute to high triglycerides.

Sedentary Lifestyle – Lack of physical activity reduces the body’s ability to burn triglycerides.

Obesity – Excess weight is linked to high triglyceride levels.

Alcohol Consumption – Alcohol is metabolized into triglycerides, raising their levels.

Medical Conditions – Diabetes, hypothyroidism, and kidney disease can contribute to high triglycerides.

How to Lower Triglycerides

Healthy Diet – Eat more whole grains, lean proteins, vegetables, and omega-3 fatty acids (found in fish like salmon).

Regular Exercise – Engaging in 30-60 minutes of physical activity daily can help lower triglycerides.

Limit Sugar and Refined Carbs – Reduce intake of sweets, white bread, and sugary drinks.

Maintain a Healthy Weight – Losing excess weight can significantly lower triglyceride levels.

Limit Alcohol and Unhealthy Fats – Reduce saturated fats and avoid trans fats.

Medication (If Necessary) – In some cases, doctors may prescribe fibrates, niacin, or statins to lower triglyceride levels.

Triglycerides vs. Cholesterol: What’s the Difference?

Conclusion

Triglycerides play a vital role in energy storage and metabolism. However, maintaining healthy levels is crucial for overall cardiovascular health. A combination of dietary changes, regular exercise, and medical management (if necessary) can help regulate triglyceride levels and reduce health risks.

Phospholipids

Phospholipids are essential lipid molecules found in biological membranes and play a critical role in nutrition, metabolism, and cellular function. They are amphipathic, meaning they have both hydrophilic (water-attracting) heads and hydrophobic (water-repelling) tails, making them crucial for membrane formation, lipid transport, and cell signaling.

chapters.title: 1. Dietary Sources of Phospholipids
chapters.content:
1. Dietary Sources of Phospholipids

Phospholipids are naturally present in many foods, especially those rich in fats.

Best Dietary Sources

Egg yolks 🥚 (rich in phosphatidylcholine)

Soybeans & soy lecithin 🌱 (a common phospholipid supplement)

Dairy products 🧀🥛 (contain various phospholipids)

Organ meats (liver, brain, kidney) 🥩 (high in phosphatidylserine and sphingomyelin)

Fatty fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines) 🐟 (source of phospholipids with omega-3s)

Nuts & seeds 🌰 (contain phosphatidylinositol)

Many processed foods contain soy lecithin, which is used as an emulsifier due to its phospholipid content.

chapters.title: 2. Metabolic Role of Phospholipids in Nutrition
chapters.content:
2. Metabolic Role of Phospholipids in Nutrition

A. Cell Membrane Integrity

Phospholipids are primary components of cell membranes, maintaining fluidity, permeability, and structure.

They regulate nutrient exchange and support cell signaling.

B. Lipid Transport & Digestion

Phospholipids aid in fat digestion and absorption by forming emulsions that break down dietary lipids.

They are key components of lipoproteins (HDL, LDL, chylomicrons) that transport fats in the blood.

C. Brain & Cognitive Health

Phosphatidylserine (PS) and Phosphatidylcholine (PC) are essential for neuronal function, memory, and cognition.

Studies suggest that dietary phospholipids may help reduce cognitive decline in aging individuals.

D. Liver Function & Fat Metabolism

Phosphatidylcholine (PC) plays a role in preventing fatty liver disease by facilitating the export of triglycerides from the liver.

It is a precursor to acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter essential for muscle control and brain function

chapters.title: 7. Phospholipid Supplements in Nutrition
chapters.content:
7. Phospholipid Supplements in Nutrition

Phospholipid supplements, particularly lecithin (soy lecithin, sunflower lecithin), are popular for their potential health benefits:

Improving cognitive function (Phosphatidylserine supplements)

Supporting liver health (Phosphatidylcholine for fatty liver prevention)

Reducing cholesterol and heart disease risk

Are Phospholipid Supplements Effective? Studies suggest that dietary phospholipids improve cognitive performance, lipid metabolism, and liver function, but whole-food sources remain the best way to obtain phospholipids.

chapters.title: 8. Conclusion: Why Are Phospholipids Important in Nutrition?
chapters.content:
8. Conclusion: Why Are Phospholipids Important in Nutrition?

Phospholipids are essential for cell membrane structure, lipid metabolism, and overall health. They:
✅ Support brain and cognitive function
✅ Aid in fat digestion and absorption
✅ Protect against fatty liver disease
✅ Improve heart and nerve health
✅ Help maintain membrane integrity in all cells

Incorporating phospholipid-rich foods (eggs, soy, fish, organ meats, dairy) or supplements can enhance overall nutrition and metabolic health

Sterols

Sterols are a class of lipids that play vital roles in cell membrane structure, cholesterol metabolism, hormone production, and vitamin synthesis. The most well-known sterol is cholesterol, but plant sterols (phytosterols) and steroid hormones are also crucial in human nutrition and metabolism.

chapters.title: 5. Plant Sterols (Phytosterols) in Nutrition
chapters.content:
5. Plant Sterols (Phytosterols) in Nutrition

What Are Phytosterols?

Phytosterols are plant-derived sterols that reduce cholesterol absorption in the intestines by competing with dietary cholesterol.

Sources of Phytosterols

Nuts & seeds 🌰

Whole grains 🌾

Vegetable oils (corn, soybean, olive) 🫒

Legumes 🫘

Health Benefits of Phytosterols

✅ Lower LDL cholesterol by 10–15% when consumed regularly
✅ Reduce heart disease risk by improving blood lipid profiles
✅ Anti-inflammatory properties beneficial for metabolic health

Studies show that 2-3 grams of phytosterols daily significantly lower LDL cholesterol levels.

chapters.title: 10. Sterols in Nutrition: Key Takeaways
chapters.content:
10. Sterols in Nutrition: Key Takeaways

✅ Cholesterol is essential for cell function, hormones, and vitamin D production, but high LDL cholesterol is harmful.
✅ Phytosterols lower cholesterol absorption and improve heart health.
✅ Sterols play a key role in bile acid formation and fat digestion.
✅ Balanced intake of dietary sterols supports metabolic health, brain function, and lipid regulation

INTRODUCTION TO HUMAN NUTRITION AND NUTRIENTS METABOLISM

Nutrient Metabolism: Understanding the Biochemical Pathways

chapters.title: 1. Overview of Nutrient Metabolism
chapters.content:
1. Overview of Nutrient Metabolism

Nutrient metabolism refers to the biochemical processes that transform macronutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, and fats) and micronutrients (vitamins and minerals) into energy, structural components, and essential molecules for physiological functions.

🔹 Key Goals of Nutrient Metabolism:
✅ Provide energy (ATP) for cellular activities
✅ Build and repair tissues, enzymes, and hormones
✅ Maintain homeostasis and biochemical balance
✅ Store and mobilize energy based on body needs

chapters.title: 2. Macronutrient Metabolism
chapters.content:
2. Macronutrient Metabolism

Macronutrients include carbohydrates, proteins, and lipids, which undergo digestion, absorption, and metabolic transformation.

A. Carbohydrate Metabolism (Glucose Metabolism)

Carbohydrates are the primary energy source for the body.
✅ Major Hormones: Insulin (lowers blood sugar), Glucagon (raises blood sugar)

🔹 Key Pathways:

⚠️ Imbalances:

Excess glucose → Stored as fat (lipogenesis)

Low glucose → Gluconeogenesis ensures a continuous energy supply

B. Protein Metabolism (Amino Acid Metabolism)

Proteins are not stored like carbohydrates and fats; they are broken down into amino acids and used for various functions.

🔹 Key Pathways:

⚠️ Imbalances:

Excess protein → Converted into glucose (gluconeogenesis) or fat

Protein deficiency → Leads to muscle loss, weak immunity, and metabolic disorders

C. Lipid Metabolism (Fat Metabolism)

Lipids are the most energy-dense macronutrients (9 kcal/g).
✅ Major Hormones: Insulin (stimulates fat storage), Epinephrine & Glucagon (mobilize fats)

🔹 Key Pathways:

⚠️ Imbalances:

Excess fats → Stored as triglycerides in adipose tissue

Low carbohydrate availability → Increases ketone production (used as alternative energy)

chapters.title: 7. Conclusion: Why Is Nutrient Metabolism Important?
chapters.content:
7. Conclusion: Why Is Nutrient Metabolism Important?

Nutrient metabolism ensures that:
✅ Cells receive energy for function and repair
✅ Hormonal balance regulates hunger, storage, and expenditure
✅ Nutrients are stored or mobilized based on needs
✅ Deficiencies and excesses are prevented to maintain health

What is metabolism?

Metabolism refers to all the chemical processes going on continuously inside your body that allow life and normal functioning (maintaining normal functioning in the body is called homeostasis). These processes include those that break down nutrients from our food, and those that build and repair our body.
Building and repairing the body requires energy that ultimately comes from your food.

The amount of energy, measured in kilojoules (kJ), that your body burns at any given time is affected by your metabolism.

Basal metabolic rate (BMR)

What is Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR)?

Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) is the amount of energy (calories) the body needs to perform basic life-sustaining functions while at complete rest. These functions include:

Breathing

Circulating blood

Regulating body temperature

Cell repair and growth

Brain and nerve function

BMR accounts for 60-75% of total daily energy expenditure (TDEE), meaning most of the calories burned each day come from BMR, even without physical activity.

chapters.title: 3. How to Calculate BMR
chapters.content:
3. How to Calculate BMR

BMR can be estimated using the Harris-Benedict Equation, which differs for men and women.

Harris-Benedict Equation

For Men:

BMR=88.36+(13.4×weight in kg) +(4.8×height in cm) −(5.7×age in years)

BMR = 88.36 + (13.4 \times \text {weight in kg}) + (4.8 \times \text{height in cm}) - (5.7 \times \text{age in years})

BMR=88.36+(13.4×weight in kg) +(4.8×height in cm) −(5.7×age in years)

For Women:

BMR=447.6+(9.2×weight in kg)+(3.1×height in cm)−(4.3×age in years)

BMR = 447.6 + (9.2 \times \text{weight in kg}) + (3.1 \times \text{height in cm}) - (4.3 \times \text{age in years})

BMR=447.6+(9.2×weight in kg)+(3.1×height in cm)−(4.3×age in years)

chapters.title: 5. How to Increase BMR
chapters.content:
5. How to Increase BMR

Although BMR is mostly determined by genetics and body composition, some ways to increase it naturally include:

Strength Training – Increases muscle mass, which burns more calories.

Eating Enough Protein – Protein has a higher thermic effect, requiring more energy to digest.

Drinking Cold Water – Temporarily boosts metabolism by making the body work harder to warm up.

Getting Enough Sleep – Poor sleep lowers metabolic rate.

Staying Active – Even small movements (fidgeting, walking) help.

Managing Stress – Chronic stress can lead to hormonal imbalances that slow metabolism.

B. Mifflin-St Jeor Equation (More Accurate for Modern Lifestyles)

🔹 For Men

BMR= (10×weight in kg) + (6.25×height in cm) − (5×age in years) + 5

🔹 For Women

BMR= (10×weight in kg) + (6.25×height in cm) − (5×age in years) −161

chapters.title: 3. Causes of Metabolic Disorders
chapters.content:
3. Causes of Metabolic Disorders

Metabolic disorders may arise due to:

Genetic Mutations – Inherited enzyme deficiencies (e.g., PKU, MSUD).

Hormonal Imbalances – Disrupts metabolism (e.g., diabetes, thyroid disorders).

Nutrient Deficiencies – Lack of vitamins/minerals affecting metabolism (e.g., iodine deficiency → hypothyroidism).

Organ Dysfunction – Liver or kidney failure affects waste removal.

Lifestyle Factors – Poor diet, lack of exercise, and obesity contribute to metabolic diseases.

chapters.title: 5. Treatment & Management of Metabolic Disorders
chapters.content:
5. Treatment & Management of Metabolic Disorders

While some metabolic disorders are incurable, they can often be managed with the right lifestyle, medications, and dietary modifications.

(A) Dietary Changes

Low-Carb Diet for Diabetes – Helps control blood sugar.

Low-Protein Diet for PKU, Urea Cycle Disorders – Prevents toxic buildup.

Low-Fat Diet for Hyperlipidemia – Reduces cholesterol levels.

Special Formulas for Infant Metabolic Disorders – E.g., lactose-free for galactosemia.

(B) Medications & Supplements

Insulin for Diabetes – Regulates blood sugar.

Statins for Hyperlipidemia – Lowers cholesterol.

Enzyme Replacement Therapy – For enzyme deficiencies like GSD.

Vitamin & Mineral Supplements – E.g., Vitamin B12 for energy metabolism.

(C) Exercise & Lifestyle Changes

Regular Physical Activity – Improves insulin sensitivity and metabolism.

Weight Management – Reduces risk of metabolic syndrome.

Avoiding Fasting in FAODs – Prevents hypoglycemia and energy deficiency.

chapters.title: 7. Conclusion
chapters.content:
7. Conclusion

Metabolic disorders affect how the body processes nutrients, leading to serious health problems if left untreated. Some disorders, like diabetes and obesity, are influenced by lifestyle, while others, like PKU and mitochondrial diseases, are genetic. Early diagnosis, dietary management, and medical interventions can help manage these conditions and improve quality of life.

chapters.content:
2. Step-by-Step Digestion of Proteins

(A) In the Mouth (Mechanical Digestion)

No chemical digestion of proteins occurs in the mouth.

Chewing (mastication) breaks proteins into smaller fragments, increasing the surface area for enzyme action.

(B) In the Stomach (Chemical Digestion Begins)

The stomach secretes gastric juice, which contains:

Hydrochloric acid (HCl):

Lowers the stomach pH (1.5–3.5), denaturing proteins (unfolding their structure).

Activates pepsinogen → pepsin (an enzyme that digests proteins).

Pepsin:

Breaks down large protein molecules into smaller peptides.

Works best in the acidic environment of the stomach.

(C) In the Small Intestine (Major Protein Digestion)

The pancreas secretes enzymes into the small intestine to continue digestion.

Enzymes involved:

Trypsin & Chymotrypsin (from pancreas): Break proteins into smaller peptides.

Carboxypeptidase: Removes individual amino acids from the peptide chains.

Peptidases (from intestinal lining): Break short peptides into free amino acids for absorption.

(D) Absorption of Amino Acids

Free amino acids are absorbed through the intestinal lining into the bloodstream.

Transported to the liver via the hepatic portal vein, where they are processed for:

Protein synthesis

Energy production

Conversion into other compounds (e.g., neurotransmitters, hormones)

Protein digestion is a well-regulated process involving the stomach, pancreas, and small intestine. It ensures that proteins from food are broken down into amino acids, which are absorbed and used for body functions such as muscle repair, enzyme production, and immune support.

chapters.title: 2. Protein Utilization Pathways

2. Protein Utilization Pathways

(A) Absorption and Transport

After digestion, amino acids are absorbed into the bloodstream through the small intestine.

Transported via the hepatic portal vein to the liver for processing.

(B) Protein Synthesis (Anabolism)

The primary function of amino acids is protein synthesis, which occurs in cells.

Types of proteins synthesized:

Structural Proteins: Muscle fibers, collagen, keratin (skin, hair, nails).

Functional Proteins: Enzymes, hormones (insulin, growth hormone), antibodies.

Transport Proteins: Hemoglobin (oxygen transport), albumin (nutrient transport).

(C) Energy Production from Proteins (Catabolism)

If the body lacks carbohydrates and fats, amino acids can be converted into energy through gluconeogenesis.

Steps:

Deamination: Removal of the amino group (-NH₂) from the amino acid.

Conversion to Glucose or Fat: The remaining carbon skeleton is used for glucose (gluconeogenesis) or fat storage.

ATP Production: Some amino acids enter the Krebs cycle to generate ATP.

(D) Conversion into Other Important Compounds

Hormones: Amino acids are precursors to insulin, glucagon, thyroid hormones.

Neurotransmitters: Tryptophan → Serotonin, Tyrosine → Dopamine & Adrenaline.

Nitrogen-containing Compounds: Used to make DNA, RNA, creatine, and heme (in hemoglobin).

(E) Excretion of Excess Nitrogen

Amino groups removed during deamination form ammonia (NH₃).

Ammonia is toxic and is converted into urea in the liver.

Urea is transported to the kidneys and excreted in urine.

Metabolic Needs: Growing children, athletes, and pregnant women need more protein.

Carbohydrate & Fat Intake: If carbs and fats are insufficient, the body breaks down protein for energy.

Health Conditions: Liver or kidney diseases affect protein metabolism and nitrogen excretion.

Conclusion

Protein utilization is essential for growth, repair, metabolism, and immune function. While protein synthesis is the primary role, excess protein can be used for energy or converted into other important molecules. Proper protein intake is crucial for maintaining muscle mass, hormonal balance, and overall health.

NUTRIENT METABOLISM: ENERGY PRODUCTION AND UTILIZATION

Nutrient metabolism refers to the biochemical processes by which the body breaks down and utilizes macronutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, and fats) and micronutrients (vitamins and minerals) for energy production, growth, repair, and physiological regulation.

chapters.title: 2. Carbohydrate Metabolism (Primary Energy Source)
chapters.content:
2. Carbohydrate Metabolism (Primary Energy Source)

Carbohydrates are the main source of energy and are metabolized through the following pathways:

(A) Digestion & Absorption

Carbohydrates (starches, sugars) are broken down into glucose in the digestive tract.

Glucose enters the bloodstream and is transported to cells.

(B) Cellular Respiration (ATP Production)

Glucose is metabolized to generate ATP (energy currency) via three main pathways:

Glycolysis (Anaerobic Process)

Occurs in the cytoplasm.

Converts glucose → pyruvate + 2 ATP.

Pyruvate enters the mitochondria if oxygen is available.

Krebs Cycle (Citric Acid Cycle)

Occurs in the mitochondria.

Converts pyruvate → Acetyl-CoA → ATP, CO₂, and NADH.

Electron Transport Chain (ETC)

Uses NADH to produce up to 34 ATP in mitochondria.

(C) Storage & Alternative Pathways

Excess glucose is stored as glycogen in the liver and muscles (glycogenesis).

If glucose is low, glycogen is broken down (glycogenolysis).

If no carbohydrates are available, glucose is made from proteins or fats (gluconeogenesis).

chapters.title: 3. Protein Metabolism (Body Building & Energy Alternative)
chapters.content:
3. Protein Metabolism (Body Building & Energy Alternative)

Proteins are not the primary energy source but are metabolized when needed.

(A) Digestion & Absorption

Proteins are broken into amino acids in the stomach and small intestine.

Absorbed amino acids are transported to the liver.

(B) Functions of Amino Acids

Protein Synthesis: Used to build muscles, enzymes, hormones, and antibodies.

Energy Production (if needed):

Deamination: Removal of the nitrogen group (-NH₂), forming ammonia.

Ammonia is converted into urea in the liver and excreted via urine.

The remaining carbon skeleton enters gluconeogenesis or Krebs Cycle.

(C) Excess Protein

If protein intake exceeds body needs, excess amino acids are converted into glucose or fat for storage.

chapters.title: 4. Lipid (Fat) Metabolism (Energy Storage & Reserve)
chapters.content:
4. Lipid (Fat) Metabolism (Energy Storage & Reserve)

Lipids (fats) provide a long-term energy source and are metabolized through the following processes:

(A) Digestion & Absorption

Fats are broken down into fatty acids and glycerol in the small intestine.

Absorbed fatty acids enter the bloodstream or lymphatic system.

(B) Lipid Breakdown (Lipolysis)

Stored triglycerides are broken into glycerol + free fatty acids.

Fatty acids undergo beta-oxidation in mitochondria to produce Acetyl-CoA.

Acetyl-CoA enters the Krebs Cycle to generate ATP.

(C) Lipid Storage & Ketogenesis

Excess fat is stored in adipose tissue (lipogenesis).

During fasting or low-carb diets, fats are converted into ketone bodies (ketogenesis), which provide alternative energy for the brain and muscles.

chapters.title: 5. Vitamin & Mineral Metabolism (Enzyme Function & Regulation)
chapters.content:
5. Vitamin & Mineral Metabolism (Enzyme Function & Regulation)

Vitamins and minerals play essential roles in metabolic pathways but do not directly provide energy.

(A) Fat-Soluble Vitamins (A, D, E, K)

Stored in fat and required for vision, bone health, and antioxidant functions.

Vitamin D aids calcium absorption for bone strength.

(B) Water-Soluble Vitamins (B-complex, C)

B-complex vitamins help in energy metabolism (glycolysis, Krebs cycle).

Vitamin C supports collagen synthesis and immune function.

(C) Essential Minerals

Calcium, Magnesium, and Phosphorus – Bone health and nerve function.

Iron – Essential for hemoglobin and oxygen transport.

Zinc – Supports enzyme functions and immunity.

Nutrient metabolism ensures that the body efficiently processes, stores, and utilizes macronutrients and micronutrients to sustain life. While carbohydrates provide quick energy, fats serve as long-term storage, and proteins support structural functions. The body regulates these metabolic processes through hormones to maintain homeostasis and energy balance.

Your TDEE is the total number of calories burned daily and includes:

Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) – Energy used at rest (~60-75% of total).

Physical Activity – Calories burned through movement (~15-30%).

Thermic Effect of Food (TEF) – Calories used to digest food (~10%).

2. Causes of Marasmus

Marasmus results from chronic starvation and severe nutrient deficiency. The main causes include:

(A) Inadequate Nutritional Intake

Lack of Calories & Protein – Due to poverty, famine, or neglect.

Poor Breastfeeding Practices – Early weaning or lack of mother’s milk.

Malabsorption Disorders – Conditions like celiac disease, chronic diarrhea, or intestinal parasites reduce nutrient absorption.

(B) Infections & Diseases

Repeated Infections (Diarrhea, Tuberculosis, HIV/AIDS) – Increase nutrient loss and reduce appetite.

Chronic Illnesses – Cancer, kidney disease, and metabolic disorders contribute to weight loss.

(C) Socioeconomic Factors

Extreme Poverty – Lack of food availability.

War & Natural Disasters – Disrupt access to food and healthcare.

Lack of Nutrition Awareness – Poor feeding practices in children.

What happens to the body in marasmus disease?

When the body is deprived of energy from food, it begins to feed on its own tissues — first adipose tissue (body fat) and then muscle. It also begins shutting down some of its functions to conserve energy. Cardiac activity slows down, causing low heart rate, low blood pressure and low body temperature. In some cases, this leads to heart failure. The immune system is also compromised, making undernourished people more prone to infection and illness and slower to recover.

Children with chronic marasmus will not have the physical resources to grow and develop as they should. They may be stunted in size or have developmental delays or intellectual disabilities. These effects can be lasting, even in children who receive treatment. Parts of the digestive system also begin to atrophy from the lack of use. This means that even when people do have food to eat, they might not be able to absorb nutrition from their food effectively. Ironically, marasmus can lead to food aversion.

10 STEPS OF WHO IN MANAGEMENT OF SERVERE ACUTE MALNUTRITION

 ( IMAM GUIDELINE)

Management and Treatment

The World Health Organization has outlined 10 steps to follow when treating severe undernutrition:

Treat/prevent hypoglycemia. Hypoglycemia can occur when calories are introduced. The rehydration formula for malnourished people includes glucose to help restore balance. It’s given incrementally during the first hours of treatment.

Treat/prevent hypothermia. Malnourished bodies have trouble regulating their own temperature, so they must be kept warm.

Treat/prevent dehydration. A special formula called RESOMAL (REhydration SOlution for MALnutrition) is given to treat dehydration in kwashiorkor. It’s designed to restore and maintain the body’s fluid/sodium balance. It can be given orally or through a tube.

Correct electrolyte imbalances. Electrolyte imbalances can have serious and even life-threatening effects, especially when a malnourished person begins refeeding. Healthcare providers try to address these first, usually in their rehydration formula.

Treat/prevent infection. With the diminished immune system that comes with kwashiorkor, all infections are serious threats to recovery. Infections are treated with antibiotics.

Correct micronutrient deficiencies. Specific vitamin and mineral deficiencies can have serious effects if they are severe enough. Healthcare providers try to correct these before refeeding.

Start cautious feeding. Undernourished bodies have altered metabolism. Refeeding will trigger their metabolism to change again. But if this happens too fast, it can cause life-threatening complications (refeeding syndrome). Feeding begins slowly under close observation. Protein, in particular, should be reintroduced gradually in kwashiorkor.

Achieve catch-up growth. Once the child has stabilized and appears to be tolerating refeeding well, their calories can increase to up to 140% of recommended values for their age. The WHO provides ready-made liquid formulas that can be given orally or by tube if necessary. This is the nutritional rehabilitation stage of treatment. It may last up to six weeks.

Provide sensory stimulation and emotional support. Children with kwashiorkor may have been in a state of apathy for some time. Their malnutrition may have stunted their intellectual, neurological and social development. Stimulating their development to reboot is part of their treatment plan. Ideally, healthcare providers will include the child’s mother in this project.

Prepare for follow-up after recovery. Before discharging the child from care, healthcare providers offer education and counseling to the mother regarding nutrition, breastfeeding, food and water hygiene and disease prevention. They may provide immunizations as necessary. If possible, they should help secure access to a consistent, nutritious food supply.
